matrices-as-functions-s1.title: A rotation and a reflection
matrices-as-functions-s1.html:
$R$ rotates the plane by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ counterclockwise and $F$ reflects it across the $x$-axis.

$$R = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right], \qquad F = \left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{matrix} \right]$$

items.q: Which matrix does "rotate with $R$, then reflect with $F$" in one step?

why.correct: Rotate first, so $R$ is on the right: $FR = \left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{matrix} \right]\left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right]$.
options: $FR$: the first move on the right.
This is $RF$: reflect first, then rotate.
This is $R^{-1}$, a clockwise quarter turn.

items.q: Which matrix does "reflect with $F$, then rotate with $R$" in one step?

why.correct: Reflect first, so $F$ is on the right: $RF = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right]\left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{matrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right]$.
options: Reflect first, so $F$ sits on the right.
This is $R$ alone; the reflection is missing.
The two moves do not cancel; $RF \ne I$.

items.q: What is the image of $\left\langle 2, 1 \right\rangle$ when it is rotated with $R$ and then reflected with $F$?

why.correct: $R\left[ \begin{matrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{matrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{matrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{matrix} \right]$, then $F$ flips the second entry: $\left\langle -1, -2 \right\rangle$. Or $FR\left[ \begin{matrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{matrix} \right]$ directly.
options: This is after the rotation only.
This is after the reflection only.

items.q: The matrix $FR = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right]$ is a single reflection. Across which line?

why.correct: $FR\left[ \begin{matrix} x \\ y \end{matrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{matrix} -y \\ -x \end{matrix} \right]$: it swaps the coordinates and negates both. Points on $y = -x$, such as $\left\langle 1, -1 \right\rangle$, stay put.
options: Reflection across $y = x$ is $RF$; it fixes $\left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle$, which $FR$ sends to $\left\langle -1, -1 \right\rangle$.
The $y$-axis reflection sends $\left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle$ to $\left\langle -1, 0 \right\rangle$; $FR$ sends it to $\left\langle 0, -1 \right\rangle$.
That is $F$ alone; the rotation changes it.

why.correct: Undo a quarter turn counterclockwise with a quarter turn clockwise: $R^{-1} = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right]$. Check: $RR^{-1} = I$.
options: Applying $R$ again turns another quarter, to a half turn.
$F$ reflects; it does not undo a rotation.
That is the output, not the input.
That is $M\left[ \begin{matrix} 4 \\ 7 \end{matrix} \right]$, the output of the output.

why.correct: $\det M = 3(2) - 1(5) = 1$. Swap $3$ and $2$, negate $1$ and $5$, divide by $1$.

items.q: What does applying $M$ twice do to $\left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle$?

options: This squares each entry; apply $M$ to $(3, 5)$ instead.
This doubles $(3, 5)$; applying $M$ again is not doubling.

items.q: By what factor does applying $M$ three times multiply areas?

mistakes.why: $\det M = 1$, not $0$; $M$ keeps areas the same.

items.q: In the product $AB\mathbf{v}$, which transformation acts on $\mathbf{v}$ first?
options: Both at once, so the order makes no difference
$AB$ and $BA$ usually differ, so the order matters.
Determinants do not set the order.

items.q: A rotation by $\frac{\pi}{6}$ counterclockwise is applied three times. Which single matrix does the same?

why.correct: Three turns of $\frac{\pi}{6}$ make $\frac{\pi}{2}$, and the rotation by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ counterclockwise has columns $(0, 1)$ and $(-1, 0)$.
options: This is one turn of $\frac{\pi}{6}$, not three.

mistakes.why: Keep the sign: $3(-2) = -6$. One flip means the composition flips.

why.correct: $\det(AB) = \det A \cdot \det B = 3(-2) = -6$: areas are multiplied by $6$, and orientation is reversed.

items.q: $L_1(\left\langle x, y \right\rangle) = \left\langle 2x, y \right\rangle$ and $L_2(\left\langle x, y \right\rangle) = \left\langle x + y, y \right\rangle$. Write the first component of $L_2(L_1(\left\langle x, 1 \right\rangle))$.

mistakes.why: That is $L_1(L_2(\ldots))$. Apply $L_1$ first: $(2x, 1)$, then $L_2$ adds the components.
$L_1$ doubles the first component first, giving $2x$.

why.correct: $L_1(\left\langle x, 1 \right\rangle) = \left\langle 2x, 1 \right\rangle$, then $L_2(\left\langle 2x, 1 \right\rangle) = \left\langle 2x + 1, 1 \right\rangle$. The first component is $2x + 1$.

items.q: Why does $P = \left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{matrix} \right]$ have no inverse function?

why.correct: Two different inputs give the output $\left\langle 2, 0 \right\rangle$, so from the output alone you cannot tell which input it came from. ($\det P = 0$.)
options: Zeros alone do not decide it; $\left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right]$ has two zeros and an inverse.
Every matrix sends the zero vector to itself.

items.q: Which transformations are their own inverses? Select all that apply.

why.correct: A transformation is its own inverse when doing it twice gives $I$.
options: Reflecting twice puts every point back.
Two half turns make a full turn.
Two quarter turns make a half turn, not $I$.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the input that a matrix $A$ sends to a known output $\mathbf{w}$ in order.
options: Check that $A$ times your answer gives $\mathbf{w}$

why.correct: An inverse must exist; then undo $A$ by multiplying the output by $A^{-1}$, and check.
